items.title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
items.content:
I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.

Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP —hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis , which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4 —a lower bound (!!) , matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log 2 7) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.

Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that !

But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N) 1/2+o(1) . The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log 0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!) . All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered , rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.

To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE —that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.

It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next. It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.

I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.

For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden. Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between. Just please don’t deny what’s happening. Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean…

items.title: New research suggests AI bubble bursting and to expect major market collapse
items.content:
A recent study covering 170 years of financial journalism reveals we are 97% likely in an AI financial bubble, and that leaders should prepare for a crash.

Financial press, rather than the stock market, predict far more crashes than occur.

Research tests how effectively the media forecasts financial bubbles and subsequent crashes.

Applied to September 2026, the research assigns a probability of up to 97 percent to being an AI bubble.

Speak to most AI investors and you will hear a level of anxiety about the current financial markets, despite record profits in recent years from the likes of Nvidia, Anthropic et al.

From the Nasdaq plunging more than 18 percent between early October and late November 2026, to worries about personal data being exposed should a glut of AI services feel the crunch and go bust , AI and markets are intrinsically linked.

For this reason, a large language model (LLM) trained to read 170 years of financial journalism from The Economist that puts the probability that AI-related shares were in a bubble in September 2026 at up to 97 percent, is prescient and timely.

Marco Grotteria of London Business School and Afonso Monteiro and Constantine Yannelis of the University of Cambridge show that the financial press often ‘cries wolf’: it warns of overvaluation every month and predicts far more crashes than occur.

The pattern recalls Paul Samuelson’s quip that Wall Street indexes, “predicted nine out of the last five recessions.” Here the financial press, rather than the stock market, predicts far more crashes than occur.

Across the 170 years, articles studied implied an average 20 percent probability of a major market crash within six months of reporting a bubble , roughly 3.5 times the actual historical frequency of 5.7 percent. The level of the warnings therefore says little. What carries information is how they rise and fall over time.

Grotteria explained what prompted the research in the first place: “Predicting bubbles is extremely difficult. A bubble occurs when prices rise above what fundamentals can justify, because investors expect to sell to someone else at a still higher price.

“But we observe neither fundamentals nor investors' expectations, so bubbles have historically been identified only ex post.

“We started thinking that by looking at the words of journalists, the sentiment of the media, we can understand whether they think there is a bubble in real time, and we can test how effectively the media forecasts financial bubbles.

“We focused on The Economist, which is a longstanding, reliable, and authoritative publication. We built our index using data from 1843, and we went all the way until 2013.”

The index was then extended with Economist articles from 2014 to September 2026.

LLMs were used to read 795,964 articles, of which around 486,000 were market relevant. Each was scored for speculative narratives, regulatory warnings, signs of speculation, valuation concerns and descriptions of boom or euphoria, which were combined into a monthly ‘bubble index’.

“The Economist talks about bubbles all the time, even in very quiet periods, so the level alone tells you little,” Grotteria says.

Discover fresh perspectives and research insights from LBS

“Every time our index goes above 40% or 50%, a bubble then the following crash happened. And in 74 percent of comparisons, the index is higher in a bubble month than in a normal one. That is where the predictability comes from.”

Leaders have reason to pay attention to a measure built on a long and consistent record of reporting, because periods of speculation matter for planning and strategy.

As Svetlana Bryzgalova , Associate Professor of Finance at London Business School, recently found, local sentiment is rarely incorporated into official economic forecasts , with the cause of business cycle fluctuations one of the “longstanding debates in macroeconomics”.

items.title: The web is losing its personality
items.content:
The Layout Maestro course is 40% off, ends soon

A look at why websites started to look the same, and how we got here.

If you browse websites created in 2026, you will have a hard time distinguishing them from each other. The differences are hard to spot, and they’re getting harder to spot every day.

In the following figure, can you spot the unique face?

You might be wondering, what unique face? Is there a mistake in the question? Nope. This is exactly what’s happening in web design right now. People think that their AI-generated design is unique, but it’s just another copy of what the AI agent already knows.

A website design should reflect its brand and values, not the LLM that produced it.

On top of that, each of us has different cultures and thoughts, so this affects how we perceive and work on designs.

For example, I will use coffee as a topic to compare. Each one of us has our own way of drinking coffee. Take a look:

Just by looking at the coffee details, you will notice each face prefers a different way. This says a lot about where they came from. However, that can change over time.

For example, I started by drinking Turkish coffee, and now I’m a full-time home barista, and espresso has become a daily part of my routine.

Your design taste changes with your life, and that is what makes your work humane. AI doesn’t have a soul/life so that it won’t have that at all. The coffee thought is one of hundreds, if not even thousands, of ideas and experiences each one of us has.

I imagine it like the following figure where the human experience is personal and based on life experiences. In contrast, the LLM one is more uniform due to it using the most common for a given problem .

If you’re one of the many who rely on AI to design for you, then you are missing a lot. I have one simple question for you: who will see and use the design you will build? Is it a human or an agent?

If you are designing for agents, you don’t need to design at all. I guess you design for people. Even if you use “UI skills” to improve the agent’s output, many people rely on the first shot and call it a day.

Here is an example of a design style that you’re probably familiar with. This is a one-shot that I prompted Claude to do.

Send payments, issue cards, and track every dollar in one place. No hidden fees, ever.

At first glance, you might say: well, this looks fine. If you view this design in isolation, yes, it might look fresh or unique, but that’s not the case here.

I imagine it like the following figure. In the center, you have the design you just used AI to create.

But the reality is, the design isn’t unique. It’s just a copy of hundreds of thousands of website designs, if not millions.

Here is the same website design I presented above, but with different content and colors. With the page blurred, you can’t tell what it is about.

Change the design options on the left, or toggle the blur and colors on the right.

Small-batch beans roasted to order and shipped within 48 hours. Your best cup starts here.

Try to unblur it and see the design. It’s the same, but with content and color changes. Where is the personality? It’s not there at all.

This is what the web has become lately. Anyone can prompt to build a landing page like this, but again, it has no personality.

Non-designers will not realize that this design is just a copy of others.

Over time, we started noticing patterns in one-shot AI landing pages. Some of them are already popular. Let’s take a look.

It’s worth mentioning that those are still valid design choices, but the overuse of them is too much when they are not needed.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임받을 이용자가 [매니저 위임 신청] 버튼으로 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 활동 중인 부매니저가 있으면 부매니저만, 부매니저가 없거나 모두 부재중이면 회원이 신청할 수 있습니다.

신청하면 갤러리 공지로 신청 글이 등록되고, 신청일로부터 7일간 찬성 댓글을 받은 뒤 운영자가 검토해 위임합니다. 첫 번째 위임 신청자가 신청한 날로부터 7일간 3명까지 동시 신청이 가능합니다.

Garage v2.6.0 released with web admin, v1.x EoL & other news

We are glad to announce the release of Garage v2.6.0 that includes a brand-new

web administration UI funded by NLnet. We also discuss many other small news:

Helm chart repository release, Garage v1.x EoL, Garage v3.0.0 beta 1 and an

outlook on upcoming work on S3 versioning.

The Garage project has been quite active lately, so we thought it would be a

good time to write a blog post to present new features and give some

Garage v2.6.0 and the web administration GUI

This is the culmination of almost two years of work by Tixie

Salander . We started this collaboration in 2024 when it

was clear that a user interface was one of the most sorely lacking feature of Garage. We

are very grateful that NLnet has again engaged with us and provided funding to

Here's a minimal example to test 2.6.0 right away:

docker run --name garage -p 3900:3900 -p 127.0.0.1:3903:3903 \

-e GARAGE_RPC_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \

-e GARAGE_DEFAULT_ACCESS_KEY=GKthisisatestkey \

-e GARAGE_DEFAULT_SECRET_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \

-v $PWD/garage.toml:/etc/garage.toml:z -v garage:/var/lib/garage \

dxflrs/garage:v2.6.0 /garage server --single-node --default-bucket

Running 2.6.0 or above, you can access the web interface on the garage admin API port, by default port

3903, so http://localhost:3903/ if you are running garage on your machine with the example above.

Logging in requires a garage admin token. The example above prints it on the command line.

If you have set the admin_token configuration variable

in your configuration file, you may use that token. Otherwise, you'll need to create a separate token

from the command line with garage admin-token create .

One world of caution: administering a remote cluster over plain HTTP is NOT safe , as

your admin token is transmitted in plain text with each request. You'll need to setup an HTTPS

reverse proxy in front of your Garage node to encrypt the connection, or/and access your

node through a VPN such as Wireguard to make sure no one can eavesdrop the credentials.

Once logged in the cluster, you will be greeted by a cluster overview screen that looks like

the following (this is a live example from our Deuxfleurs cluster):

The web interface follows a similar pattern to the CLI: cluster monitoring,

layout configuration, bucket and access credential management are all available

as you expect. Here are example videos (now included in the Quick Start guide

as well) showing the setting up of a new cluster from scratch:

From a development standpoint, the web UI currently lives in a separate Git

report any issues there and not in Garage's main issue tracker. Tixie will

continue being the maintainer of the UI moving forward.

Official Helm chart published in our public repository

This has also been one of the longstanding requests from our Kubernetes users, and it's

now done! Starting today you can deploy Garage on Kubernetes easily thanks to our

self-hosted Helm repository. Both "regular" (tgz+index.yml) helm chart repository as well as OCI artefacts

are available. Instructions in the documentation

Thanks to Boris M. and Maximilien for contributing this improvement to Garage,

along the many contributors that participated in finding the right way to make this work.

The Garage helm chart follows its own version scheme, with the current version being 0.10.7.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites: This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
items.content:
In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.

If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.

“The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.

This announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the company wide latitude as it works through these remaining issues.

For example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight.

The authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. items.content:
Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.

It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.

Identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.

Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.

To install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases . Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.

VSCode - In Settings, search Font Family, then specify Intel One Mono

Sublime Text - Go to Sublime Text -> Preferences -> Settings and set font_face to Intel One Mono

IntelliJ Platform - Go to File -> Settings -> Editor -> Font and set Font to Intel One Mono

We recommend the .otf or .ttf format for desktop use.

The .ttf files are also well suited for mobile apps.

The .woff and .woff2 fonts are optimized for web use.

We recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.

Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:

Programming Ligatures: To use programming ligatures, activate the ss01 feature (Stylistic Set #1). Additional refinements are available via ss02 and ss03 : Stylistic Set #2 switches the <= and >= combinations to arrow forms (math contractions being the default otherwise), and Stylistic Set #3 additionally activates a “www” ligature.

Alternate three: New in release 1.5. Alternate form for three added. The round top three, numerator, denomenator, superior and inferior can be activated with stylistic Set #4.

Raised Colon: The colon is automatically raised in operators, to align with math symbols. For non-programming contexts, the raised colon can be applied contextually between numbers or activated generally. The contextual option is available via ss11 (Stylistic Set #11); for the global switch use ss12 (Stylistic Set #12) or salt (Stylistic Alternates).

Language Support: ccmp and locl features ensure correct display across a wide range of languages. These are usually active by default. We recommend setting the language tag/setting in your software to the desired language for best results.

Superior/superscript and inferior/subscript figures are included via their Unicode codepoints, or you can produce them from the default figures via the sups (Superscript) and subs / sinf (Subscript) features.

Fraction numerals are similarly available via the numr (Numerator) and dnom (Denominator) features. A set of premade fractions is also available in the fonts.

Activating Programming Ligatures in Code Editors

Programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:

VSCode - In Settings, add "editor.fontLigatures": "'ss01'"

Sublime Text - In Settings, add "font_options": ["ss01"]

You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. items.title: How WinHelp files work
items.content:
I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp .hlp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp , a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.

Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt , which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco . Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.

A .hlp file starts with the magic number 3F 5F 03 00 , followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: |SYSTEM holds the title and settings, |TOPIC holds the text, |FONT holds the fonts, |CONTEXT holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like |bm0 .

The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.

All the text lives in |TOPIC , which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.

Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a new topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.

WinHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, says whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:

let pair = u16 ::from_le_bytes([input[pos], input[pos + 1 ]]) as usize ;

let mut back = cursor. wrapping_sub (pair & 0xfff ). wrapping_sub ( 1 );

The length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, x followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes xxxxxx .

One fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.

On top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.

WinHelp 3.1 keeps the table in |Phrases . In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:

let code = 256 * ( usize ::from(ch) - 1 ) + usize ::from(next);

out. extend_from_slice ( self . phrase (code / 2 ));

The lowest bit of the code says whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.

The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across |PhrIndex and |PhrImage . Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in 01 starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, 011 starts a run of literal bytes, 0111 means a run of spaces, and 1111 means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte.

items.title: Over 7,000 Creators Push Back Against Australia’s Proposed AI Copyright Opt-Out
items.content:
More than 7,000 Australian creators demand opt-in consent before AI firms can train on their photos, writing, or music

Under Australia’s current copyright framework, permission belongs to the creator or the rights holder. The proposed opt-out model would flip that: AI developers could use protected works by default, while each rights holder would have to discover the use and actively object.

That reversal has drawn more than 7,000 photographers, writers, musicians, and other creators to sign a statement demanding that their work be used for AI training only with explicit permission.

Creator organizations argue that an opt-out system transfers the costs of monitoring and enforcement from well-funded AI companies to individual rights holders.

All 23 member organizations of the Creators’ Rights Alliance signed a letter urging the Australian government to reject any opt-out mechanism, according to the alliance. Their core argument is that the burden of monitoring, enforcement, and objection would fall on creators rather than on the companies profiting from the data.

Isabelle Doran, CEO of the Association of Photographers and vice chair of the Creators’ Rights Alliance, made that point directly to Australia’s attorney general. She argued that individual creators cannot match the negotiating leverage or technical resources of major AI companies . An opt-out system, she wrote, places the burden on creators only after their work has already been used.

Australia’s Copyright Agency has echoed that concern, arguing in parliamentary proceedings that opt-out would transfer responsibility from AI users to rights holders, inverting the existing structure of copyright law.

The government has ruled out one specific form of AI copyright exception, but several licensing alternatives remain under active consideration.

The government has ruled out a broad text-and-data-mining exception, but it is still considering licensing models that could allow AI training without permission from every individual rights holder. What remains unsettled is whether a statutory licensing arrangement could achieve a comparable outcome under different legal framing.

A statutory licensing model could authorize AI training on broad categories of copyrighted material under government-set terms. Fees would be collected and distributed through a central system, though the precise structure, payment mechanism, and opt-out process have not been finalized.

Critics, including the Copyright Alliance, have warned that such a system could effectively replicate the access a broad exception would provide. They argue it would do so while presenting itself as a form of compensation. Attracting overseas AI investment has been reported as a government objective, but whether an opt-out or statutory framework would achieve that remains unestablished in the available reporting.

Indexing visual works at scale requires no direct notice to the photographer, leaving creators especially exposed under a default-access system.

Images are easily copied and incorporated into datasets without notifying the original photographer . An opt-out system would require each creator to identify uses, submit valid reservations, and monitor whether those reservations were honored.

Doran’s letter to the attorney general warned that the proposed mechanism could broaden the ability of overseas AI companies to commercially exploit photographers’ work without consent and could threaten their livelihoods.

Australia’s debate is part of a wider international conflict over whether AI training requires direct permission from rights holders or can proceed under statutory or compulsory licensing.

Rights-holder groups have called for voluntary, opt-in licensing that preserves creators’ ability to set terms, control scope, and negotiate price. items.title: Effective Neovim setup for agentic coding towards 2027
items.content:
Hey, what's up? It's Takuya here. In this article, I'm going to share my new Neovim setup, which I built from scratch with an AI agent.

GitHub - craftzdog/dotfiles: My personal dotfiles

My personal dotfiles. Contribute to craftzdog/dotfiles development by creating an account on GitHub.

In the previous setup I shared in 2023 , I used LazyVim to avoid maintaining plugins, and it's been working great.

Thanks to the LazyVim community, I could easily keep my plugins up to date and tweak the settings.

But the more I customized it, the more unstable it got.

Fixing errors after every LazyVim update was kind of annoying.

Meanwhile, recent Neovim releases have added a lot of built-in features that used to need plugins:

vim.lsp.enable and after/lsp/<name>.lua : LSP setup with almost no boilerplate

:restart : reloads Neovim and restores the session

So I decided to build a fresh setup on top of them.

The agentic coding paradigm shift has arrived, and I've adapted to an agentic workflow .

These days, I mainly use Neovim to review code , rather than to write it by hand.

To be honest, I don't know how long I'll keep using it, since workflows are changing so fast.

But I thought it would be interesting to share my current setup.

Tweaking a Neovim config is super easy now, because you just tell your agent what you want.

So instead of writing Lua, I wrote a spec of my config in English on Inkdrop , and fed it to my agent step by step via the MCP server .

Spec note The spec describes what I want and why , not how .

Ask the agent to implement only that step.

Reload Neovim with :restart and check the behavior myself.

Read the spec and implement only the step I name. Add nothing beyond it.

Check your work lightly: Neovim starts without errors: nvim --headless +qa

Don't build test projects or drive the UI. I check the behavior myself after the restart.

Neovim restarts in the same terminal and restores the windows, tabs, and buffers.

Save first with :wa . Unsaved buffers block the restart. Or use :restart +qall! to discard them.

After a step that adds a plugin, vim.pack shows an install prompt. Confirm it.

Run the agent in a separate terminal split, not in a :terminal inside Neovim, since the restart kills it.

Feel free to copy it and feed it to your own agent, and tweak it to your taste.

Neovim 0.12 or newer. The config relies on built-ins that landed in 0.12: vim.pack , vim.lsp.enable , and the ui2 message UI.

nvim-treesitter 's main branch builds parsers locally

Mason installs most language servers through npm

Back the text search and the file finder

A Nerd Font. I use PlemolJP Console NF. Icons appear in the tabline, statusline, completion menu, and file explorer, so a plain font shows boxes.

I started by telling the agent where the spec lives:

I'd like to make a neovim setup. I'm going to write a spec in this note: <link to the spec>

~/.config/nvim : the config root folder init.lua : enables vim.loader for faster startup, then requires these files directly, in order: craftzdog.utils , assigned to the global Craftzdog

craftzdog.config.options , .keymaps , .autocmds , .commands , .workarounds

lua/craftzdog/ : my config lives here utils/ : shared helpers init.lua : returns a table of helper modules, empty for now. Later steps add modules like utils/editor.lua , exposed as editor .

config/ : plain Neovim settings, one file per name above

plugins/ init.lua : installs every plugin in one vim.pack.add call, then requires each group file

Each plugin group gets its own file next to it (e.g. ui.lua ), which configures its plugins with require("<plugin>").setup({ ... }) .

keymaps.lua : every keymap that uses a plugin, required last so all plugins are set up first. Group files hold no keymaps.

Lua files are indented with tabs, formatted by stylua with its defaults.

Generated file tree 1.2 Leader and basics

Clipboard is unnamedplus , so yank and paste go through the system clipboard.

Indent is 2 spaces : tabstop ,…

items.title: Collection of preserved UI style guides
items.content:
This is a collection of preserved UI style guides a.k.a. interface guidelines from various companies, starting from the early 1980s and continuing to today.

(Commodore) Amiga was a multimedia personal computer particularly popular in the 1980s and 1990s in Europe. Its GUI was called Workbench.

Android is a mobile operating system and a rival to iOS. The first style guide I could locate was in 2012.

BlackBerry was a beleagured maker of mobile handsets.

Common Desktop Environment (CDE) is a desktop environment for Unix machines, using (and eventually merging with) OSF/Motif widgets.

Common User Access (CUA) is a late 1980s standard for user interfaces that influenced Windows and OS/2.

Graphics Environment Manager (GEM) is a 1980s operating system/GUI. It was well-known by users of the Atari ST computers, known in these circles as TOS .

GNOME is a desktop environment for Linux and BSD operating systems. Note that the versioning number of these guidelines is very confusing.

iOS (previously iPhone OS) is Apple’s mobile operating system for iPhone smartphones and their siblings.

Java is a programming language, which comes equipped with JFC (Java Foundation Classes) and Swing GUI components.

These are some historical Apple GUI style guides, starting with Lisa in the 1980, and continuing to the “classic” Mac OS, with a brief stop in the Apple II corner.

More modern Apple Mac style guides, covering Mac OS X/Aqua and beyond.

An abandoned mobile operating system designed by General Magic .

Guidelines specific to Microsoft Office, in particular covering the use of its ribbon .

NeXTSTEP was NeXT’s influential operating system and graphical user interface. It eventually morphed into OpenStep on one side, and modern Mac OS X on another.

Apple Newton was Apple’s PDA launched in 1993 and abandoned in 1998.

Nokia released various style guides for its early smartphones, including its Symbian operating system.

OPEN LOOK is a UNIX graphical user interface, started by Sun and AT&T.

Palm OS was the original graphical operating system for Palm’s mobile devices. Eventually, the company moved toward webOS , covered elsewhere on this page.

PenPoint was an early tablet operating system developed by GO Corporation for its unsuccessful line of devices.

RISC OS is a British operating system and GUI, developed originally for Acorn computers, and continuing as a community project.

Style guides for various UNIX-based operating system from SGI , or Silicon Graphics Inc. Just like CDE above, these too use the Motif widgets.

Taligent was a troubled software company, incorporated as an Apple/IBM partnership. One of its fruits was a CommonPoint application framework.

webOS was a successor to Palm OS that was eventually purchased by HP and later LG Electronics. Today, it is used on smart TVs, refrigerators, and projectors.

Does Microsoft Windows need an introduction? Note a little hole here around 1990, where Microsoft was preoccupied with CUA framework in partnership with IBM.

Style guides for failed mobile Windows efforts, starting with Windows Mobile 6 , and continuing through Windows Phone 7.

That’s it! Please let me know if you have any thoughts and particularly if you have some style guides that are missing from the above list.

items.title: Entering the Geminispace
items.content:
On May 1st, 2020, Project Gemini made the rounds for the first time via a Hacker News discussion thread . I remember seeing the announcement back then, barely a month after the Covid 19 worldwide lockdown, and thinking it was a cool gimmick. But that was that.

However, I’ve recently been seeing a few gemini:// links here and there as footers in hand-crafted blogs, and I nerd-snipped myself to export this blog as a Gemini capsule that you can find at gemini://capsule.jmmv.dev/ . The process has been fun, and I actually quite like the extreme minimalism of the resulting site. So what else would you expect from me? I had to write about it—hence this post.

Today we’ll learn a little bit about what Gemini is, how I approached the blog export to its native gemtext format, and I’ll confess a couple of… sins I committed along the way.

A blog on operating systems, programming languages, testing, build systems, my own software

projects and even personal productivity. Specifics include FreeBSD, Linux, Rust, Bazel and

A terrible name, that is. Looking for information about Gemini these days is extremely hard, thanks to Google polluting the namespace with its own AI offering. Of course that’s not Project Gemini’s fault because Google’s thing came after them, but still, good luck finding stuff about this network.

Joking aside, let’s look at Project Gemini’s barebones front page:

Project Gemini's front page, displayed in the Lagrange browser. … and break down the introductory and only paragraph:

Gemini is a new internet technology supporting an electronic library of interconnected text documents.

You can think of Gemini as a way to access a bunch of text-only pages, with links among them, so you can find information and follow links to additional resources. Instead of using http:// or https:// URL prefixes, you use gemini:// instead.

That’s not a new idea, but it’s not old fashioned either.

Exactly. Gemini is like the WWW , or “the web” in more colloquial/modern parlance. In fact, Gemini is a parallel community to the web. Obviously, that’s not a new idea because the web dates back to 1989, and we are now 37 years after that.

The idea is not unique either because Gopher , a much lesser-known option, exists as well. Surprisingly to me, I realized that Gopher came after the web in 1991 while researching this article. I had always assumed Gopher was first and that the web came to replace it because of Gopher’s rigidness. But that’s not quite what happened.

It’s timeless, and deserves tools which treat it as a first class concept, not a vestigial corner case.

Humans have shared written documents since around 3400–3100 BCE (roughly 5,100–5,400 years ago) in ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, and that’s probably (hopefully?) not going away. It’s true, though, that at this point, text sharing is not the primary thing that the web does, as you well know. We have morphed the web from a document distribution tool into an app platform, for better or worse.

A little confession: I worked at Google for 12 years, starting right at the time they published Google Wave (2009), which to me marked the start of truly interactive web apps—more so than Gmail (2004) did. In the back of my mind, I knew I was helping turn the web into how we run apps, destroying the traditional desktop paradigm—a feeling I never liked. And… it happened. Obviously, it’d have happened without me, a little pawn in the game, but it bothered me regardless.

Gemini isn’t about innovation or disruption, it’s about providing some respite for those who feel the internet has been disrupted enough already.

(That comma splice hurts.) As we have established earlier, Gemini’s ideas are not new, so it’s indeed not innovative. And seeing how little people read these days, or even how unable to pay attention to long-form text they are, it’s not going to disrupt anything either. But respite is key: having a separate place where you know you’ll only find some sort of counter-culture sounds…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: A new study has found that the largest U.S. data centers use four times as much power as Los Angeles
items.content:
A new study co-authored by a UCLA Fielding School of Public Health researcher has found that over the course of a year, the largest data centers in the United States use four times as much power as the city of Los Angeles. Findings also indicated that such centers’ electricity consumption and carbon emissions rival those of some U.S. states.

The study, published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Sustainability, examined hyperscale data centers (HDCs), the largest and most powerful class of data centers that support services such as cloud computing, large language model training and global deployment of artificial intelligence tools.

The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of HDCs’ electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions since the rise of AI. The authors include researchers from Harvard University and Falco Bargagli Stoffi, an assistant professor in the UCLA Fielding Department of Biostatistics.  They compared their findings on power usage to electricity sales by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP), which serves approximately 4 million Angelenos.

“Our central estimate suggests that the 403 hyperscale data centers we studied across the United States used nearly four times as much electricity as LADWP sells to its customers in a year,” said Bargagli Stoffi, adding that the analysis attributed more than half, or 54%, of the centers’ electricity use to fossil fuels.

The study was one of the first to combine fragmented data, helping to better paint a picture of the emissions of individual facilities. “Better public information on electricity use would help communities and policymakers assess the environmental consequences of this industry’s growth,” Bargagli Stoffi said.

The researchers noted substantial regional differences, with some HDCs relying much more on carbon-intensive electricity than others. Many of the facilities were concentrated in geographic areas where electricity is heavily generated by coal-fired power plants. The study found that four states — Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa —accounted for more than half of the electricity use studied.

Read more about the study and how researchers are planning to quantify health impacts at UCLA Fielding’s website.

items.title: Nextcloud Office Desktop app
items.content:
On June 9, 2026, we released the first production-ready version of Euro-Office , a sovereign collaborative office suite developed and governed in Europe. With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer , we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version of the app is available for download. It lets you work offline, switch between Nextcloud Hub in your browser and the app on your computer, and get the same experience on Windows, macOS and Linux.

In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. Featuring editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, it offers high compatibility with Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP). Connect it to Nextcloud Hub to edit files with your team in real time.

The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:

With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.

Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.

How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:

Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!

Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.

The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.

Keep in mind that you need a digital certificate to sign documents. To obtain one, you can ask your IT team at work, or get one for personal use from a trusted provider. You can find providers approved in the EU in this list .

In the Protection tab, you can also set a password for a file, or limit what others can do: comment, fill in forms, or edit with tracked changes only.

You can find and download the latest version of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app from our official installation page .

You can also find unsigned builds of Euro-Office desktop app and build the app from the source yourself by following the instructions on GitHub .

We want to keep improving the app. You are welcome to share any issues you find with our engineering team on GitHub.

items.title: In defense of lock poisoning in Rust (2025)
items.content:
There’s recently been some discussion about the benefits and downsides of lock (mutex) poisoning in Rust, spurred by a recent proposal to make the default mutex non-poisoned, i.e. silently unlock on panic (see also, recent discussion on Hacker News ). As a passionate defender of lock poisoning, I thought I’d gather and write about my thoughts on this matter.

Rust, like most multithreaded languages, has mutexes : a construct to ensure that a particular piece of data can only be accessed by one thread at a time. The way mutexes work in Rust is particularly well-considered:

This is all quite reasonable! Let’s look at an example that processes incoming messages for a set of tracked operations. Let’s assume that multiple threads could be processing messages, so we have to guard the internal state with a mutex. (We’ll discuss alternative approaches to this problem later.)

This is a very typical use of mutexes: to guard one or more invariants or properties of some kind. These invariants are upheld while the mutex is unlocked. In this case, the invariant being guarded is that Operations::ops has complete and up-to-date tracking of all in-progress and completed operations.

Of equal importance is the fact that, while the mutex is held, the invariant is temporarily violated . In order to process the message, we have to remove the state from the map, create a new state, then put it back into the map. During this period, Operations::ops is missing this one operation, so it no longer tracks all operations. But this temporary violation is okay, because no other threads see this in-between state. Before the mutex is released, this code is responsible for putting the operation back into the map.

Is it always true that the operation is put back into the map? Unfortunately not always, in the presence of what I think of as unexpected errors . Many practitioners draw a separation between two different kinds of errors that a system can have. The terms recoverable and unrecoverable are sometimes used for them, but I tend to prefer the following terms (see also some discussion by Andrew Gallant ):

Generally, in Rust, expected errors are handled via the Result type, and unexpected errors are handled by panicking . Now, there isn’t a firm requirement that things be this way.

But in typical production-grade Rust, expected errors are Result s while unexpected errors (and only unexpected errors) are panics. Lock poisoning is built around this assumption.

Consider what happens if a panic occurs in OperationState::process_message . This depends in part on the build flags and surrounding code, so let’s look closely at all the possibilities. In Rust, there are two ways to configure build flags on panic:

Some real-world applications (such as most of what we ship at Oxide ) abort on panic, but most of this post is actually moot for aborts. So in the rest of this post, we’re going to focus on the default unwind behavior.

If a panic is invoked in the context of a catch_unwind , an Err(E) is returned, where the value E is whatever message or other payload the panic occurred with.

If there’s no catch_unwind , and the panic occurs on the main thread, then a message is printed out and the program exits with an error.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027
items.content:
Car buyers in New York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year.

“People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor said.

In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee.

We end users might not like having to open our wallets each month, but the capital markets sure do, and car companies love making the capital markets happy. Which is why there has been such a push toward connected vehicles. Remote start and predictive maintenance alerts are nice, but your regular payments to the car company— plus any data of yours it can sell —is the goal.

Some automakers have gone even further. Infamously, BMW and its heated seats. Like the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit, it’s a fact half-remembered; BMW North America never tried such a thing, just in countries like South Korea and the UK , and in 2023 BMW’s board said that subscriptions would only be for software-related features from then on.

New York’s press release mentions heated seats but also calls out a number of other modern tech features: “enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.”

But the way the actual law is written appears to leave a rather large loophole, at least to these eyes.

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

A heated seat might not have “an ongoing cost,” but the maps and databases that enable “enhanced navigation” and “hands-free driving” systems definitely do, as these need to be constantly updated. A regular cadence of software updates also generates an ongoing cost to an OEM, arguably. And car companies pay for plenty of lawyers who really love to argue.

And so, while experiments like BMW’s seat heater subscription won’t be allowed in the state, the new rule might still allow for plenty of ongoing fees for services like OnStar or Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro system we tested recently .

items.title: Mistakes Will Be Made: designing safer software for real people
items.content:
Keep the spoken sentence in the Top Middle Bottom Playback speed ×1.0 ×1.1 ×1.2 ×1.3 ×1.4 ×1.5 ×1.6 ×1.7 ×1.8 ×1.9 ×2.0

Table of contents An electronic immobilizer stops a car starting without the right key. A 2025 study found that US models fitted with one saw theft fall roughly 80% against comparable models without it. The improvement didn’t require the driver to become a detective.

Much of what we call user error in software is a design failure that shows up later, when someone makes an ordinary mistake. People will click the wrong link, trust a familiar name and approve a payment while thinking about dinner. That’s predictable, so the series asks: why do we still build software where one ordinary mistake can break everything, and what can we do about it? It looks at why being careful isn’t enough, what security advice costs and who pays for it, how screens and even protection software set traps of their own, who’s responsible when protection is skipped, and what to build instead.

The short answer to the first half: the people who build software often aren’t the ones who pay for the mistake. A carmaker that skips a known protection faces recalls and lawsuits. Software makers mostly don’t, and EU liability rules treat software as a product only from December 2026. A 2001 paper said it in one line: expect trouble wherever the party able to protect a system isn’t the party that suffers when it fails.

As for what to do about it, I’d borrow the order medical-device safety guidance already uses, with design first and warnings last: prevent the dangerous action where practical, contain the damage when it happens, and help people with the decisions that remain.

Bank branches close. Government services move into apps. Paper forms disappear. Millions of people are expected to use systems they didn’t choose, and their details also sit in other people’s systems, beyond their control.

Strong technical protection doesn’t close every route through a person. A help desk can be persuaded to reset access. A user can be talked into running a command or approving a payment. AI makes the lure cheaper and more convincing. And people fall fast: in phishing tests, the typical person who falls for it types in their data about 50 seconds after opening the email.

Training doesn’t fill the gap on its own. A 2025 UC San Diego study of nearly 20,000 employees found no measurable benefit from annual training, and a small benefit from short lessons shown right after a test click. A typical fake campaign fooled about one employee in ten, yet by the eighth month more than half had clicked at least once, and an attacker needs only one. Well-run continuous programmes can help at work, but someone using a banking app at home can’t depend on an employer running one. Fear appeals and gotcha tests can push people away from security, and shame stops many victims reporting, so reporting a mistake has to stay easy and safe. Constant expert vigilance can’t be a condition of ordinary use. Part 1 has the attacks and the studies.

Every instruction costs attention. An active user can have more than a hundred accounts and faces hundreds of tips nobody ranked for them, and stress, which scammers create on purpose, leaves even less attention to spend. A 2009 Microsoft Research paper argued that ignoring much of that advice is economically rational: the time it costs everyone can outweigh the direct losses it prevents. It’s a rough illustration, not a full account, but the point stands: advice has a price, and someone pays it.

The same step can cost much more to someone with an old device, little technical confidence or nobody to ask. Hardware keys, phones that stop getting updates and protection sold only on pricier plans cost real money too. Growing up online doesn’t make anyone immune: younger adults report losing money to scams more often than older ones, though older victims lose more when they do.

So universal advice has to justify its cost, and the better…

items.title: Minipg: PostgreSQL as a Single Executable
items.content:
minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure.

its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it,

and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it.

A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.

minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with

h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor,

with h9's Plan 9 kernel answering their system calls.

There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.

It needs JavaScript Promise Integration,

which Chrome and Edge have from version 137;

The demo runs minipg's Linux build, which runs inside the Postgres image itself.

It starts Postgres as ordinary processes and serves on a unix socket,

New databases come from a template cluster made at build time,

because initdb takes half a minute on v86.

A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password)

and pgdata/ , Postgres's data directory as plain files.

A stopped one can be copied like any directory.

New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale,

In CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices:

without /dev/kvm , h9 runs Postgres on its native backend.

Exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb , enforced by a lock.

It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image

and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb .

The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start.

Commands never host Postgres themselves.

If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it.

psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine

(about 90 ms to start) over the same root.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: AMD-specific fork of llama.cpp
items.content:
tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV.

As of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc.

The rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own.

Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc…

These new forks generally all have a few things in common:

They focus on a specific subset of models and/or hardware

They use a frontier model to vibe-code the entire thing

They chase ever-higher token generation speeds

… and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model , on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate.

In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster.

Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last.

That said, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy.

Enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts . It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds.

I appreciate llama.cpp’s approach to software development. They are a stable base to branch off from. Contributions are vetted throughly and applied judiciously. ✅

The rdna-boosts repo is a set of small patches that are applied to base llama.cpp. Fewer moving parts mean fewer things to maintain ✅

The changes are (somewhat opaquely, it’s all straight Claudish 😬) outlined in the documentation, ensuring some degree of transparency. ✅

If you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published.

podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1

This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server:

"ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1" \

My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the important lines.

I imagine upgrading would be pulling a new image down, though I have not tried this yet.

On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled:

Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next.
